steps.title: Revalidate update bytes before cache shortcuts
preconditions: Run the public tracer app -- test services updates command in its owned isolated Miniflare/R2 process. Original test lines 1–240 and all original 42 requests remain unchanged; six appended requests use the original 48-request limit. Worker source is unchanged and checked byte-for-byte.

The original synthetic fixture leaves a valid artifact whose in-memory Ed25519 signature can be verified, and an unsigned-key object whose metadata digest deliberately differs from the filename digest. The new conditional header matches that filename digest, so returning 304 before metadata validation would be observable.

Only synthetic fixture R2 mutation is used: delete the known mismatched object, prove absence with an isolated read, and restore the original valid stable pointer. Feed and valid artifact bytes remain intact. No production/private data, credentials, external requests or persistent publication.

Assertions cover the local origin HTTP response. They do not invalidate an already cached CDN/client copy, establish broad ETag parsing, rehash streamed archive bytes inside the Worker, certify a native package, execute release tooling or test storage errors.
actions: Finish the original 42-request publication and acceptance-namespace journey; send a matching filename-digest validator to the known metadata-mismatched artifact by GET and HEAD.
Delete only that synthetic object, verify its absence, and send the same matching validator by GET.
Send the now-stale validator to the intact signed synthetic artifact; verify full downloaded bytes and signature. Send its correct validator by HEAD and check 304 body/header behavior.
Restore the original valid stable pointer and GET its feed with the exact matching feed ETag; verify fresh 200 byte-identical signed payload and no-store headers.
Finish at exactly 48 requests, zero outbound attempts and unchanged production Worker source; dispose the owned process and temporary R2 state.

expectations.description: A matching filename-digest If-None-Match must not bypass R2 metadata or existence checks: metadata-mismatched GET and HEAD return 503 with no ETag and no-store, then the deleted object returns exact 404/Not found with no ETag and no-store. The GET error is exact Release artifact unavailable.; HEAD has no bytes. The corrupt object exists before its first two requests. These are origin revalidation checks, not revocation of previously cached bytes.

A mismatching validator on the valid inert artifact returns 200 with exact downloaded bytes, ephemeral Ed25519 verification and exact size. Matching HEAD returns bodyless 304 with no Content-Length. Both responses retain exact artifact ETag, application/zip, immutable one-year cache policy, attachment filename and no Retry-After. Conditional list, weak, wildcard, Range and CDN behavior are not covered.

After synthetic restoration of the valid stable pointer, a matching feed validator still returns 200 with the exact signed feed bytes, digest ETag, XML content type and no-store. The matching feed validator does not produce a conditional 304; the complete payload is still returned. GET transport Content-Length is not asserted; byte equality is the oracle. No live signing identity, publisher, CDN, native install or Sparkle is involved.

mappings.why: The valid stable pointer resolves to its hash-checked feed before the response ignores conditional caching and returns exact signed bytes with no-store. Existing malformed-pointer coverage is retained, not newly claimed.

Only a valid artifact route reaches object lookup and metadata matching. Matching validators cannot shortcut missing/mismatched objects because these guards run first; both R2 head and get paths are exercised.
Valid artifact responses carry immutable-cache headers. Mismatching GET returns full bytes; exact matching HEAD returns 304 after validation, with Content-Length removed.
The valid artifact response exposes exact streamed body bytes for a mismatching validator; matching HEAD is intercepted above. No large-file memory bound or arbitrary Range behavior is proven.
